plan_document:
Rural Diagnostics Uptake Consortium: Existing Research Plan

The consortium will examine variation in use of the battery-powered HemoCheck hemoglobin test across twelve rural primary-care clinics in Kijani District. The study focuses on whether technical reliability, clinic operations, and local care practices explain why some devices are incorporated into everyday work while others remain stored. Fieldwork will begin before the district's planned anemia screening campaign and continue for six months.

Research questions
1. How do assay performance, battery charging, reagent storage, calibration, and maintenance affect whether HemoCheck is available and trusted at clinic level?
2. How do supply-chain reliability, staffing, screening workflows, and referral capacity affect routine use of HemoCheck?
3. How do clinicians, community health workers, patients, and local referral networks understand anemia testing and make decisions about testing and follow-up?

Aims
The project will produce a comparative account of device readiness and everyday use across clinics, identify operational bottlenecks that can be addressed by the district health office, and describe how social authority and local care pathways shape uptake. Findings will be used to recommend a feasible implementation package for the screening campaign.

Tasks
1. Priya Nanduri (biomedical engineering) will bench-test assay sensitivity against the district laboratory analyzer, record battery performance, review calibration logs, and assess reagent storage conditions at all twelve clinics.
2. Daniel Okoro (public health) will map reagent ordering, delivery intervals, stockouts, staffing, screening throughput, and formal referral pathways; he will obtain monthly clinic records for the six-month study period.
3. Laila Mensah (anthropology) will conduct observation and interviews with nurses, laboratory aides, community health workers, patients, and traditional birth attendants to document decision-making, illness concepts, and informal referral networks.
4. Priya, Daniel, and Laila will jointly classify clinics as high, intermittent, or low users based on recorded test volume and device-readiness measures.
5. Daniel will convene a district feedback workshop to develop recommendations for battery support, reagent distribution, training, and referral coordination.

old_questions.question: How technical readiness—assay performance, battery charging, reagent storage, calibration, and maintenance—affects HemoCheck availability and trust at clinic level.
How supply chains, staffing, screening workflows, and referral capacity affect routine HemoCheck use.
How clinicians, community health workers, patients, and referral networks understand anemia testing and decide on testing and follow-up.

new_questions.question: How does a time-limited, externally supported maternal-health program create or fail to create durable clinic ownership of point-of-care anemia testing after support is withdrawn?
How are authority, responsibility, and follow-up for women with suspected anemia allocated among outreach staff, clinic staff, and patients when NGO support is ending?

ground_truth.what_changed_and_why: The first two plan questions are replaced: technical readiness is no longer the central explanation, and district-wide screening operations are no longer a relevant implementation setting. The third question is retained but narrowed to ownership, authority, and follow-up in maternal care. This change follows the postponement of the anemia campaign, the end of central cartridge procurement, the concentration of cartridge access in four NGO-supported clinics, evidence of acceptable device functioning, and evidence that use depends on outreach presence and uncertain treatment or confirmatory care.

speakers.name: Dr. Priya Nanduri
speakers.background: Priya is a biomedical engineer with four years of postdoctoral work on point-of-care diagnostics in district hospitals and rural primary-care settings. She has conducted bench validation against reference analyzers, battery and environmental stress testing, usability observation, and maintenance-log audits for low-power blood-testing devices. She joined the consortium to determine whether apparent nonuse reflects genuine device failure, preventable maintenance problems, or factors outside the instrument itself.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya treats a diagnostic device as a material system with measurable operating conditions: cartridges, storage, power, calibration, operator steps, and quality control. The early evidence that the supported clinics have acceptable assay agreement and functioning hardware makes her wary of broad claims that the test itself explains variation. She wants the revised work to establish a credible technical baseline at the NGO-supported sites and to specify what maintenance responsibility would actually transfer when external support ends. She is skeptical of explanations based only on narratives unless they can be tied to observable workflow conditions and concrete consequences for device availability.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Dr. Laila Mensah
speakers.background: Laila is a medical anthropologist with nine years of ethnographic research experience in maternal health, frontline nursing, and referral practices in East African primary-care systems. She has managed multi-site qualitative fieldwork using participant observation, semi-structured interviews, care-pathway tracing, and collaborative field-note review. As project manager, she coordinates field access, ethics procedures, and the integration of qualitative findings with the consortium's operational evidence.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Laila examines uptake as a question of who is authorized, expected, and able to act after a test result. For her, a HemoCheck result has little practical meaning if routine staff do not control cartridges, treatment, confirmation, or referral follow-through. She is especially interested in how the outreach team's presence can temporarily organize responsibility, and what happens to pregnant women when that arrangement disappears. She frames the revised study around ownership, professional boundaries, trust, and the lived pathway from suspected anemia to treatment rather than around device use alone. She relies on Priya and Daniel for technical and system-level claims outside her direct evidence.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Daniel Okoro
speakers.background: Daniel is a public-health implementation researcher with seven years of experience designing service-delivery studies for maternal and child health programs. His work combines facility record review, supply-chain mapping, service-readiness assessment, referral-pathway analysis, and implementation timeline reconstruction. He has worked with district health offices and nongovernmental organizations to translate findings into practical transition plans, including plans for commodity handover and continuity of treatment.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Daniel sees the new problem as an implementation and continuity-of-care failure shaped by financing, procurement authority, treatment availability, and the approaching withdrawal of a parallel program. He argues that the relevant unit is no longer all twelve clinics or a future screening campaign, but the four NGO-supported clinics and the maternal care pathway they currently sustain. He wants clear dates, quantities, responsible institutions, and plausible transition scenarios: when cartridges stop, whether iron treatment is available, where abnormal cases go, and which actor owns each handoff. He is confident that structured mapping of these delivery arrangements will produce actionable options for the district and future programs.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

He also reports that HemoCheck cartridges are no longer procured centrally; the remaining clinics that use the test obtain cartridges through a maternal-health nongovernmental organization serving only four of the twelve sites. transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: Sorry, I’m a couple of minutes late—where have you got to? I was hoping today we could look at whether the campaign delay changes what this study ought to be about, because I’ve had some fairly major news on the cartridge—on the cartridge supply.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: We’ve only just started, so perfect timing. Before we decide the campaign delay changes everything, I’m really keen to hear the cartridge news, and also what the NGO is actually covering at those four sites besides cartridges, like maintenance, transport, staff time, that sort of thing...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: The campaign is postponed for at least a year because the external funding for reagents was withdrawn, and central procurement of HemoCheck cartridges has ended. The NGO is now the only route I can see for cartridges, and that's at four clinics only. I don't yet have a clean answer on maintenance, transport, or staff support, or even their firm, firm end date. That's what we need in writing before we assume those four sites are comparable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Laila Mensah
transcript.text: That makes the four sites a pretty different object of study, doesn't it? In the early conversations, people were already describing the test as the outreach team's work, even where the nurse was perfectly comfortable doing the finger-prick. It was what happened after a low result that seemed to stop them. Daniel, do the records tell us whether iron and confirmatory testing have actually been unreliable for pregnant women, or is that more uneven than staff are saying—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: Not cleanly enough to say yet. The clinic registers show iron is patchy, but they don't reliably distinguish a stockout from a woman being told to buy it elsewhere, and confirmatory testing is barely visible in the facility records. I think we need to trace a few actual low-result, low-result cases when outreach isn't there, because the gap may be after the test rather than the test itself.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Laila Mensah
transcript.text: I'd want those cases to include the handoff, not just whether the woman reached a referral point. Who told her what the result meant, whether anyone expected the nurse to arrange something, whether she was sent to buy iron. That’s probably where responsibility gets passed around. I need to check the consent and access side if we follow women beyond the clinic, but it feels like the right place to look.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That would help explain the blank days I saw at that one NGO clinic. The unit passed its checks and there were cartridges in the cupboard, so if routine testing stops when outreach leaves, I’d be reluctant to call that readiness, I mean, meaningful readiness. Laila, when you trace those cases, could you also note who’s actually expected to run the device on an ordinary clinic day?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Laila Mensah
transcript.text: I can do that. I’d ask it a bit indirectly too, like who normally takes it out, who feels they can decide to test, and then who owns the result once it’s low. Because “the outreach team’s work” may not mean they lack the skill. It may mean nobody wants to promise the next step on a day when iron or confirmation isn’t there, and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: And that makes the supply map less like background and more like the thing we need to map. For each of those four sites, I’m wondering if we put the ordinary-day pathway next to the outreach pathway, so cartridges, who runs it, iron, confirmation, referral, and who pays or transports. If one link disappears when the NGO team leaves, that tells us quite a lot about—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: I think that side-by-side is useful, but I’d add the very basic device chain too. Where it’s stored, who charges it, who does the control check, and who they call when it flags an error. Otherwise we may find an ordinary-day pathway that looks complete on paper, but the machine is effectively only available when the NGO person is there. I need to see whether the maintenance logs actually, actually distinguish that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: Those are all handoffs we should put on the same timeline. Not just whether the device works today, but what the NGO supplies, what the clinic can sustain alone, and the date each piece is meant to, um, stop. Priya, do your logs show whether control checks are actually being done by clinic staff or only during NGO visits?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: Not consistently, at least from the first pass. The logs usually say a control was done, but not who did it, and a few entries line up suspiciously closely with the NGO visit dates, so I can't infer clinic ownership from them yet. I'd want to check the four sites' logs against the visit schedules before we, we build too much on that distinction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: That cross-check matters, because it lets us separate a device the clinic owns from one the NGO happens to operate on clinic premises. I’ll try to get the visit schedules and the written support terms at the same time. Then we can lay those against the logs and the low-result— the low-result pathways, though I’m not yet sure the NGO records will be complete.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Laila Mensah
transcript.text: Mm. And when we do the case tracing, I’d be careful not to treat a missing NGO record as just missing data. The woman may have been told to go somewhere else, or waited because she couldn’t pay or travel. Could we get enough from the visit schedules to pick out a few ordinary clinic days around those visits, instead of only comparing whole months, and then—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: If we anchor the tracing on, say, a few days right before and after each NGO visit, we can see whether testing and the follow-up chain actually change when they’re present. I’ll need the visit dates and probably the outreach register, not just the clinic monthly totals. The awkward bit is matching a low result to treatment or referral without exposing women’s records unnecessarily, but we can, can work out a minimal case-tracing sheet.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Laila Mensah
transcript.text: The minimal sheet should leave room for the woman’s account without turning it into a surveillance exercise. We may find a “referral” is really just advice to travel or purchase something. Or rather, it may not be an arranged next step at all. I’ll check what consent wording and permissions we’d need before we decide how far that tracing can go.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: Mm, yes, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: It may be worth treating the records themselves as part of the handoff problem. If the NGO register, clinic register, and referral book can't tell the same story for a small set of cases, that isn't just an analytic nuisance. It tells the district there is no continuity mechanism to inherit. I'll see what identifiers or dates, dates we can use without pulling more personal information than we need.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Laila Mensah
transcript.text: I’d avoid starting from the records as though they define the case, because some women may never appear in the referral book at all. If we use dates and a very small set of clinical details just to locate possible handoffs, then ask staff and, where consented, women what actually happened, that- that feels less intrusive and more likely to catch the informal routes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: We can use the records to identify a possible episode, not to declare that the episode is complete. And the first thing we need from the NGO is really their end date, delivery schedule, and whether iron, transport, or referral support ends with cartridges, because otherwise we can’t tell the district what would actually have to be picked...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Laila Mensah
transcript.text: Right, that’s the missing piece.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: From my side, I need the NGO to say whether their support covers the unglamorous bits, controls, replacement batteries, troubleshooting, not just cartridge deliveries. If that all disappears on the same date, a clinic might still have a working HemoCheck in the cupboard but no defensible way to keep it in use. I’ll cross-check those four maintenance logs against the visit dates once Daniel has them.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: I don't think we should wait to settle the whole redesigned study before asking for that. I'll request the NGO's support terms, the visit and delivery schedules, and a clear statement of what ends when. Cartridges, iron, transport, controls, all of it. Then we can see whether the four clinics are really sustaining a service, or- whether they're just hosting an outreach activity.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: Yeah—without that, we can’t call it clinic-level readiness.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Okoro
transcript.text: Okay, I think we can stop there and give everyone a few minutes back. Thanks, both. I’ll come back once I’ve heard from the NGO, and then we can pick this up.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Laila Mensah
transcript.text: Thanks, Daniel. Speak soon.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: All right, bye both.
